items.prompt: Identify what each of the four factors of production means in an operation.
items.canonical_answer: Land: the natural resources the operation draws on - the site, the water, and the minerals, crops, timber or fish taken from nature. Labour: the physical and mental effort of the people employed, whose value depends on skill, training and motivation as well as numbers. Capital: the man-made assets used to produce other goods and services - machinery, buildings, vehicles, tools - and the money committed to acquiring them. Enterprise: bringing the other three together and bearing the risk that the venture loses money.
marking_guidance: One mark-worthy point per factor: the four must be distinguished, not listed.
Capital must be the man-made productive assets, not simply "money".
Enterprise must carry the risk-bearing element, not only "the owner".
A recall card: it asks for all four factors, which the papers ask for one item at a time, so it carries no paper tariff.

items.prompt: A Walvis Bay company catches and freezes hake. It holds a fishing quota, runs two trawlers and a freezing plant, employs 90 crew and processors, and is owned by a family who borrowed to buy the second trawler. Identify the factor of production each of those resources represents, and explain which one the business would find hardest to replace.
items.canonical_answer: The quota and the hake stock it gives access to are land, because they are a natural resource. The 90 crew and processors are labour. The two trawlers and the freezing plant are capital, as is the borrowed money committed to them. The family deciding to borrow and carrying the loss if the catch or the price falls are supplying enterprise. The hardest to replace is the quota: crew can be recruited and a trawler can be bought or chartered, but the quota is issued in limited quantity by the authorities and the company cannot create more of it, so its output is capped by that factor whatever it does with the other three.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use this company's own resources, not a generic list.
Reasoning: the mechanism linking quota to capped output must be given, because that is why it binds.
Conclusion: the answer must reach a single named factor as the hardest to replace.

items.prompt: Explain how a rise in the cost of labour can change the mix of factors of production a manufacturer uses.
items.canonical_answer: Dearer labour raises the cost of every unit of output that is made by hand, so the cost gap between doing the work with people and doing it with equipment narrows. Where the technology of the process allows a machine to do what a person was doing, the business may substitute capital for labour: it buys equipment, uses fewer employees per unit, and converts what was a wage cost into the cost of owning and running the machine. The substitution is limited by that proviso. A cutting table can be mechanised; the judgement of a quality inspector or the personal contact a customer is paying for substitutes far less readily, so in those parts of the operation the higher wage is absorbed or passed on rather than designed out.
marking_guidance: Mechanism: the answer must explain why relative cost drives substitution, not simply assert that it does.
The limit on substitution - whether the technology allows one factor to do the other's work - must be stated, because the conclusion holds only where it does.

items.prompt: Correct this statement: "Capital means the money a business has, and enterprise means the owner."
items.canonical_answer: Both halves are loose. Capital as a factor of production means the man-made assets used to produce other goods and services - machinery, buildings, vehicles, tools and equipment - together with the money committed to acquiring them. Money sitting in an account has produced nothing; it becomes capital when it is turned into productive assets. Enterprise is not a person but a function: bringing the other three factors together and bearing the risk that the venture loses money. It may be supplied by an owner, but in a large company it is supplied by managers acting for the shareholders, who are the ones actually carrying the risk.
marking_guidance: Both errors must be corrected, not one.
Capital must be identified as productive assets rather than cash balances.
Enterprise must be identified as a function - combining the factors and bearing risk - rather than a job title.

items.prompt: Define the transformational process.
items.canonical_answer: The transformational process is the sequence by which an operation converts inputs into outputs that are worth more to a customer than the same inputs were worth separately.

items.prompt: Identify, in order, the three stages of the transformational process and what belongs in each.
items.canonical_answer: Stage one, inputs: the four factors of production, plus bought-in materials and components, information such as orders and specifications, and in many services the customer. Stage two, transformation: the work done on those inputs, which may change a physical form, move something to where it is wanted, hold it until it is wanted, or change its condition or ownership. Stage three, outputs: the goods or services sold, and also by-products, scrap and waste, which carry disposal or reworking costs of their own.
marking_guidance: The three stages must be given in order: inputs, transformation, outputs.
What you need at the start - the factors of production plus bought-in materials and information - must be named as the input data of the process.
Each step must be stated with what happens in it, not merely labelled.
The result must include waste and by-products as well as saleable output; an answer ending with saleable output only is incomplete.

items.prompt: A private clinic in Windhoek sees patients, runs tests in its own laboratory and dispenses medicines. Explain one way in which its transformational process differs from a factory's.
items.canonical_answer: The clinic's key input is the patient, and its transformation changes the patient's condition rather than the form of a material, as a factory's does. Because the customer is inside the process, the clinic cannot produce in advance or hold its output in stock: a consultation or a test happens only when the patient is there. So it has to match doctors, nurses and laboratory capacity to when patients arrive, whereas a factory can build up stock in quiet weeks and sell it later.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - the patient is an input, and the transformation changes the patient rather than a material.

2 marks (AO2): the reasoning applied to the clinic - because the customer is inside the process, the work cannot be done in advance or stocked, so capacity must match arrivals; 1 mark for a generic services point.
Context: the clinic's own facts. Conclusion: a clear difference from the factory case.

items.prompt: Explain why an operation measures its output against a standard and feeds the result back.
items.canonical_answer: The purpose is correction. A process that is not measured cannot be corrected, because nobody knows which part of it has moved. Comparing what comes out - quantity, quality, time taken, cost - against the standard set for it identifies a gap, and feeding that result back lets the business change either the inputs it uses or the steps of the transformation itself. A brickworks finding one batch in twenty cracking can dry the clay longer, which changes an input, or lower the kiln temperature, which changes the transformation. Without the measurement neither response is available, and the waste - which is also an output, and a costed one - carries on being produced.
marking_guidance: The reason must be correction of the process, not record-keeping for its own sake.
The answer must show why feedback enables a change to inputs or to the transformation.

items.prompt: A brickworks fires 42 000 bricks a week at a total cost of N$294 000. Last quarter 40 000 of them were saleable; this quarter only 38 000 are, because more are cracking in the kiln. Explain the effect of that change on the business.
items.canonical_answer:
The cracked bricks have already consumed the full set of inputs: the same clay, the same labour and the same kiln fuel as the sound ones. Cost is incurred at the point of firing while revenue is earned only at the point of sale, so a brick that fails after firing carries its whole cost and earns nothing back.

The effect is therefore on cost per saleable brick rather than on total spending, which is unchanged at N$294 000. Last quarter that was N$294 000 / 40 000 = N$7.35 a saleable brick; this quarter it is N$294 000 / 38 000 = N$7.74, a rise of N$0.39 on every brick the works can actually sell. At an unchanged selling price the margin on each brick narrows by that amount, and the works also has 2 000 more cracked bricks a week to crush or remove. Because the firing is irreversible, the only response available is at the input or the transformation - drying the clay longer, or lowering the kiln temperature - which is why the proportion cracking is measured and fed back at all.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the works' own figures - 42 000 fired, the change from 40 000 to 38 000 saleable, and the N$294 000 cost.
Reasoning: the mechanism must be that cost is incurred at production while revenue comes at sale, so failed units carry full cost.
Conclusion: the answer must reach the rise in cost per saleable brick, calculated, and the narrowing margin that follows.

context.situation: rising kiln failure rate

items.prompt: A furniture maker sells a table for N$3 400. The timber, glue, screws and varnish bought in for each table cost N$1 250 in total, and no other bought-in materials or components go into it. It sells 60 tables in a month. Calculate the added value per table and the total added value for the month.
items.canonical_answer: Added value per unit = selling price per unit - cost of bought-in materials and components per unit = N$3 400 - N$1 250 = N$2 150 per table. Total added value = added value per unit x units sold = N$2 150 x 60 = N$129 000 for the month. The N$129 000 is the money the operation itself generated and is what the business has available to meet wages, rent, power and every other cost before anything is left as profit.
marking_guidance: Formula: added value per unit = selling price - bought-in materials and components per unit.
Substitution must be shown for both the per-unit and the monthly figure.
Units: the currency must appear on every figure, and the monthly total must be stated for the period.
Interpretation: one sentence saying what the added value is available for; it is not profit.

items.prompt: A tannery in Otjiwarongo sells raw hides for N$180 each, of which N$95 is the cost of the hide bought from the abattoir. It is considering dyeing and finishing the hides instead, which would let it sell them at N$320 while raising the bought-in cost to N$130 because of the dyes. Explain what this does to added value and why the business might still hesitate.
items.canonical_answer:
Added value now is N$180 - N$95 = N$85 a hide. Finished, it becomes N$320 - N$130 = N$190 a hide, so added value more than doubles, rising by N$105 on every hide. The gain comes from both directions of the formula working together: the price rises by N$140 while the bought-in cost rises by only N$35.

The hesitation is that added value is not profit. Dyeing and finishing needs vats, drying space, water, power and trained staff, and none of those appear in the added value calculation because they are not bought-in materials or components. The extra N$105 a hide is what is available to pay for them. Whether the move is worth making depends on whether those costs come to less than N$105 a hide at the volume the tannery actually sells, and on whether buyers at N$320 exist in the numbers assumed.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the tannery's own figures on both sides of the change.
Reasoning: the mechanism must show added value rising because price rises by more than bought-in cost.
Conclusion: the answer must reach the point that the extra added value has to cover the new processing costs before any of it is profit.

items.prompt: A leather workshop buys N$95 of leather for every pair of sandals it sells, because eight per cent of each hide is lost as offcuts. New cutting patterns would cut that loss to four per cent, saving N$4 of leather on each pair. It sells 400 pairs a month at N$260. Explain the effect on added value.
items.canonical_answer:
The leather is a bought-in material and is paid for whether it ends up in a saleable product or in the offcut bin, so waste raises the bought-in cost carried by each pair actually sold. Cutting the loss reduces that subtracted term while the selling price is untouched, and added value is the gap between the two.

Added value per pair now = N$260 - N$95 = N$165. With the new patterns the bought-in cost falls to N$91, so added value becomes N$260 - N$91 = N$169, a rise of N$4 a pair. Over the month that is N$4 x 400 = N$1 600 of extra added value.

Because the wages, rent and power that the added value has to cover have not changed, the whole N$1 600 falls through to profit - which is why waste reduction is worth more to this workshop than a price rise of the same size would be, since a price rise risks losing sales and this does not.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the workshop's own figures - the N$95, the N$4 saving and the 400 pairs.
Reasoning: the mechanism must be that bought-in material is paid for whether sold or wasted, so the subtracted term falls.
Conclusion: the answer must reach the monthly figure and the point that it falls through to profit.

items.prompt: Two learners are asked about the contribution of operations to added value. One answers "added value is the profit the business makes". The other answers "contribution is selling price minus variable cost". Correct both.
items.canonical_answer: Neither is right for this topic. Added value is not profit: it is the amount left after the bought-in materials and components are paid for, and it still has to cover wages, power, rent, marketing and finance before anything remains as profit. A business can have large added value and no profit at all. And the word contribution is being used here in its ordinary sense - the part operations plays in creating added value - so it carries no formula. Selling price minus variable cost per unit is the costing sense of contribution, which belongs to the costs topic and is a different quantity. A question about the contribution of operations to added value is asking what operations does, not for a calculation.

The first correction must identify what added value still has to cover.
The second must identify contribution here as the ordinary sense of the word, with no formula applied.

items.prompt: Analyse why an operation that improves on one of the four measures may worsen on another.
items.canonical_answer: Start from the condition that the four measures are computed from different quantities: one from resources used per unit, one from objectives met, one from output per unit of input, one from the long-term claim on resources. The mechanism is that a single change to the process usually moves more than one of those quantities, and not in the same direction. Running a bottling line faster raises output per employee, so productivity improves; it also gives each bottle less time in the filling head, so the proportion rejected rises, and resources used per saleable bottle rises with it, which is a fall in efficiency. The measurable consequence is that a business reporting only the productivity figure sees an improvement while its cost per saleable unit has gone up. The effect reaches profit, because the scrapped bottles consumed materials and labour, and it reaches the customer if the rejects escape into what is delivered. That is why managers read the measures together and weight them according to the objectives set for the period.
marking_guidance: Condition: the four measures are computed from different quantities.
Mechanism: one process change moves several of them, and not all in the same direction.
Consequence: a named pair moving in opposite directions, with the effect on cost per saleable unit.
The chain must reach profit or an identified stakeholder, and must say why using one measure alone is the risk.

items.prompt: A Walvis Bay fishing company has raised its catch per vessel this season by taking more hake than the stock can replace. Explain the difference between productivity and sustainability as tests of this operation.
items.canonical_answer: Productivity measures output per unit of input over a stated period, so it says how hard the inputs are working now; sustainability asks whether the operation can be carried on into the long term, using natural resources no faster than they are replaced. items.prompt: Analyse the risk a business runs if it manages its operations on efficiency alone.
items.canonical_answer: Start from the condition that efficiency is computed as resources used per unit of output, so any change that lowers the numerator improves the figure regardless of what it does to the product. The mechanism is that the cheapest ways of lowering resource use are often reductions in the thing the customer is buying: thinner materials, fewer checks, less time with each customer. The measurable consequence is that average cost per unit falls and is reported as an improvement, while returns, complaints and repeat orders move the other way with a delay, because customers discover the change after they have bought. The effect reaches the objective the operation was set - a clinic measured on cost per patient can meet its target while failing to treat patients correctly - and it reaches revenue once buyers respond. The counter-effect that could reverse the conclusion is that where the resource being removed genuinely adds nothing the customer values, such as material lost as offcuts, efficiency and effectiveness improve together.
marking_guidance: Condition: efficiency is a ratio that improves whenever resource use falls, whatever else changes.
Mechanism: the cheapest resource reductions often reduce what the customer is buying.
Consequence: reported cost per unit improves while the objective is missed, with the lag in customer response identified.
The chain must reach the objective set for the operation or an identified stakeholder, and should note the case where the two measures move together.

items.prompt: Correct this statement: "A business with the lowest costs in its industry is the most effective."
items.canonical_answer: That describes efficiency, not effectiveness. Low cost per unit is a statement about the ratio of resources to output. It can also meet every objective while spending more than it needed to, in which case it is effective and inefficient. A further caution on the cost figure itself: average cost only indicates efficiency where quality and the product mix are unchanged, so the lowest cost in an industry may be the cheapest product rather than the best-run operation.

items.prompt: An Okahandja factory produces 2 000 units a week with 20 employees. It adds a night shift of 10 people, and weekly output rises to 2 700 units. Explain the difference between production and productivity, using these figures.
items.canonical_answer: Production is the total quantity produced in a period; productivity is that quantity divided by the input used to produce it. The factory's production has risen from 2 000 to 2 700 units a week. items.prompt: Analyse how a rise in productivity feeds through to a manufacturer's costs.
items.canonical_answer:
Start from the condition that the price paid for the input has not risen by as much as the output has. The mechanism is arithmetical at first: cost per unit is the input cost divided by the output it produces, so if the same wage bill produces more units, the wage cost carried by each unit falls. A firm paying N$126 000 a month for 2 160 cabinets carries N$126 000 / 2 160 = N$58.33 of labour in each; at 2 520 cabinets on the same bill it carries N$126 000 / 2 520 = N$50.00.

The chain only reaches a lower total cost under a second condition: the extra output has to be sold, or the input has to be reduced in step with it. If the firm can sell only 2 160, the extra 360 cabinets sit as unsold inventory having consumed timber and hardware, and the business is worse off despite the better ratio. And if the productivity rise was bought with a pay rise in the same proportion, the wage bill rises with the output and cost per unit is unchanged. Where both conditions hold, the consequence reaches profit through a wider margin at the same price, or reaches market share if the firm passes the saving on.
marking_guidance: Condition: the input price must not have risen in the same proportion as output.
Mechanism: input cost divided by a larger output gives a smaller cost per unit, shown arithmetically.
Consequence: the second condition - the extra output is sold or the input is reduced - must be stated, with what happens when it fails.
The chain must reach the profit or competitive position of the business.

items.prompt: A clothing factory is offered a productivity bonus scheme that would pay machinists 15% more for 20% more output. Evaluate whether it should introduce it.
items.canonical_answer:
It should introduce the scheme only if it can sell the extra output, and on those figures that is the question the decision turns on. The arithmetic favours it: paying 15% more for 20% more output lowers labour cost per garment, because the wage bill rises by less than the quantity it produces. That is the decisive criterion - the relationship between the pay rise and the output rise - and it is satisfied here.

The criterion is not sufficient on its own. Higher productivity becomes a lower total cost only where the extra garments can be sold, or the workforce reduced in step. A factory already selling all it makes converts the scheme into profit; one that is producing to a fixed order book converts it into unsold stock bought at a 15% higher wage bill, which is worse than doing nothing.

The strongest argument against is quality. A bonus paid on quantity gives machinists a reason to work faster and check less, so the count of garments may rise while the count of saleable garments does not; the scheme needs a quality condition attached, or the rejects will consume the saving. The judgement therefore depends on the order book and on whether reject rates can be monitored per machinist. With firm demand and measurable quality, introduce it; with a fixed order book or no way of attributing faults, hold off and spend on training or equipment instead, which raises output without paying for speed.

Context: the answer must be argued on the 15%-for-20% figures given, not on bonuses in general.

Counterargument: the quality risk from paying on quantity must be addressed.

items.prompt: Analyse the effect on a food processor of installing equipment that recovers heat from its cooking line.
items.canonical_answer:
Start from the condition that the recovered heat replaces a genuine quantity of purchased fuel, and that the processor goes on operating long enough to collect the saving. The mechanism is direct: heat taken from the outgoing product and put back into incoming water is heat not bought, so the fuel bill falls by the amount recovered. That saving repeats every month the equipment runs, which is what distinguishes it from a one-off gain. The measurable consequence is a lower cost per tonne processed, which either widens the margin at the current price or lets the processor quote below a competitor still paying the full fuel bill.

The equipment is paid for before any saving arrives, the line is down during installation so output is lost, and the processor may borrow to fund it. items.prompt: A Namibian fish processor is considering committing to certified sustainable sourcing for its whole catch. Evaluate whether it should.
items.canonical_answer:
It should commit if it is selling, or seriously intends to sell, into markets where certification is a condition of entry - and it should not commit on general principle if it is not. The decisive criterion is market access rather than cost saving, because certification does not reduce what the processor spends; it changes who will buy from it.

The case in favour is that some retail chains, exporters and public bodies set environmental conditions on the suppliers they buy from, so certification may widen the market the processor can reach and may protect the volumes it already has if an existing buyer adopts such a policy. It may also help recruitment and retention where employees place a value on it, and it reduces the risk of the stock itself being fished beyond recovery, which would end the business regardless of its accounts.

The case against is that certified sourcing usually costs more per tonne than the alternative, so it can raise the cost of every unit the processor sells rather than lower it, and that is a continuing cost rather than a one-off outlay. There is also audit and record-keeping to fund.

On balance the judgement turns on evidence about buyers: firm indications from named customers that they require it, or a price premium they will pay. With that evidence, commit. Without it, the processor is paying a permanently higher input cost for a benefit it cannot yet identify, and the better course is to certify one product line and test the response before committing the whole catch.

items.prompt: Explain the benefit of consistency in a capital intensive operation.
items.canonical_answer: Machinery repeats the same action to the same tolerance for as long as it is maintained, while a person repeating the same action varies with fatigue, attention and skill. So a capital intensive operation tends to produce more uniform output, with fewer defects and less reworking, and that develops in two directions. Fewer rejects means less material and labour spent on units that are not sold, which lowers cost per saleable unit. And uniformity can be promised: a supermarket taking a weekly pallet to a fixed specification is buying the consistency as much as the product, so for that customer it is often the decisive benefit rather than the cost one.
marking_guidance: The benefit must be developed beyond "machines are consistent" to what the consistency is worth.
The answer must reach both the cost effect and the customer effect, because they are different benefits.

items.prompt: Explain the limitations that follow from the size and timing of the outlay in a capital intensive operation.
items.canonical_answer: The money is committed before any of the output is sold, so the business carries the risk of a forecast that has not yet been tested. Once spent, the outlay becomes a cost that must be covered whatever level of output is achieved: a firm that borrows to install a line and then meets weaker demand than it expected still makes the repayments, and the cost spread over fewer units raises average cost exactly when revenue is falling. The commitment is also hard to reverse - equipment sold second-hand fetches less than it cost, and a business cannot reduce it the way it can reduce a wage bill by releasing staff. On top of that the equipment loses value through wear and through newer models coming onto the market, so the business can be left running a line that still works while competitors run cheaper ones.
marking_guidance: The limitation must be developed through the mechanism: fixed cost spread over fewer units when demand disappoints.
The answer must reach the irreversibility of the commitment, since that is what distinguishes it from a labour cost.

items.prompt: Analyse what happens to a capital intensive manufacturer's cost per unit when demand falls by a third.
items.canonical_answer: Start from the condition that most of this operation's cost is the equipment, which is paid for at the same rate whether the line runs full or half. The mechanism is that cost per unit is total cost divided by output, so when output falls and the larger part of total cost does not fall with it, the quotient rises. A plant with N$600 000 a month of equipment cost making 30 000 units carries N$600 000 / 30 000 = N$20 of equipment cost in each; at 20 000 units it carries N$600 000 / 20 000 = N$30, a rise of N$10 a unit with nothing about the process having changed. The measurable consequence is that margin narrows at the same selling price, and the firm may reach a loss at a level of demand a labour intensive competitor would survive, because that competitor can release staff and cut its largest cost in step with the fall. The effect reaches the profit of the business and, if the shortfall lasts, its ability to meet the repayments on the equipment.
marking_guidance: Condition: the larger part of total cost does not fall with output.
Mechanism: cost per unit is total cost divided by output, so the quotient rises, shown arithmetically.
Consequence: margin narrows at an unchanged price, with the comparison to a labour intensive competitor.
The chain must reach the profit of the business or its ability to service the borrowing.

items.prompt: A juice plant fills bottles by hand with 20 workers paid N$5 500 a month. An automated line would cost N$2 400 000 and need 4 operators on the same pay. Demand is seasonal: the plant runs near capacity for nine months and at about a third of it for three. Evaluate whether the plant should automate.
items.canonical_answer:
On the wage arithmetic alone the case looks strong: 20 x N$5 500 = N$110 000 a month now against 4 x N$5 500 = N$22 000, a saving of N$110 000 - N$22 000 = N$88 000 a month, so N$2 400 000 / 88 000 = 27.3 months to recover the outlay before any allowance for power, maintenance and interest. Recommendation: automate, but only if the seasonal quarter can be used or the finance is arranged over a term long enough to survive it.

The decisive criterion is what happens in the three slack months. Wages can be reduced when demand falls, by not renewing seasonal contracts; the N$2 400 000 cannot. So the automated plant carries its largest cost through a quarter in which it produces a third of its output, and the payback is slower than 27.3 months because the saving is smaller in those months. The strongest argument the other way is consistency and capacity: an automated line fills to a uniform standard and can raise output quickly when the season turns, which may win the very contracts that fill the quiet quarter.

The judgement therefore changes with two things. If the plant can find off-season work - a contract pack for another brand, or a second product - the seasonal objection falls away and automation is clearly right. If it cannot, and the finance is short-term, the better course is a partial move, automating the filling head while keeping labour on packing, which takes part of the saving for a fraction of the commitment. It is also worth weighing that the sixteen people released are a significant employer's contribution to a small town's income, which may matter to the owners and to their standing with local customers.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a recommendation is required, with the condition attached to it.
Context: the answer must be argued on this plant's figures and its nine-and-three seasonal pattern.
Criterion: the decisive factor is the behaviour of the two cost types in the slack quarter.
Counterargument: the consistency and capacity advantages of the line must be addressed.
Condition: the answer must name what would change the judgement - off-season work, or the term of the finance.

items.prompt: Explain why flexibility is a benefit of labour intensive operation.
items.canonical_answer: People can be moved between tasks and re-instructed within a day, where equipment set up for one specification has to be re-tooled or reprogrammed. That develops into a commercial advantage wherever the work arriving is varied or irregular: a workshop taking forty different gate designs in a month can put the same welders on all forty, quoting for each, while a programmed line would need a changeover for every one and would refuse most of the orders. The flexibility extends to scale as well as to specification. Because the initial outlay is small, the operation can be expanded or contracted without committing or stranding large sums of capital, so a business facing uncertain demand carries less of the risk that it has built for a volume that does not arrive.
marking_guidance: The benefit must be developed into a commercial consequence, not left as "workers are flexible".
The answer must reach both specification flexibility and scale flexibility, because they are separate advantages.

items.prompt: Explain the limitations of a labour intensive operation as output volume rises.
items.canonical_answer: Labour cost per unit tends to be higher at large volumes, because each additional unit takes roughly the same paid time as the last, where a machine's cost is spread more thinly the more it makes. So a labour intensive workshop that competes comfortably at 600 units a month may be undercut at 6 000 by a mechanised rival whose equipment cost per unit has fallen while its own has not moved. The exposure to wages compounds it: costs rise directly whenever wage rates rise, through negotiation, minimum wage changes or competition for skilled staff, and there is little in the operation to absorb the increase. Output also varies with absence, turnover, fatigue and individual skill, so uniform quality is harder to hold and harder to promise to a customer buying to a specification.
marking_guidance: The limitation must be developed through the mechanism of cost per unit at volume, with the contrast to equipment cost made explicit.
The answer must reach the exposure to wage rises and the variability of output, so that the limitation is more than a cost point.

items.prompt: A safari lodge in the Zambezi region employs guides, cooks and housekeeping staff and charges N$3 200 a night. Explain why it remains labour intensive even though it could automate check-in, cleaning schedules and ordering.
items.canonical_answer: What the lodge sells is largely the labour itself. A guest paying N$3 200 a night is paying for a guide who reads the bush, food cooked to order and rooms attended to personally, so labour is the factor that creates the value rather than a cost of delivering it, and equipment substitutes for it only in part. Automating check-in and the ordering system removes administrative time, which is worth doing, but it touches the part of the operation the guest is not buying. Automating the guiding or the service would remove the thing being sold, and the lodge would be competing on price against operations with lower costs. The flexibility matters too: guests arrive in varying numbers with varying requirements, and staff can be redeployed across tasks in a way a fixed system cannot.

items.prompt: A clothing manufacturer in a country where labour is plentiful and equipment must be imported is deciding whether to stay labour intensive as it grows. Evaluate the decision.
items.canonical_answer:
It should stay largely labour intensive while its output stays varied, and move selectively as particular lines become high-volume and standard. The decisive criterion is the volume and variety of the output rather than the cost of labour in the abstract, because it is volume that lets equipment cost be spread thinly enough to beat a wage bill.

The context strengthens the case for labour on both sides of that comparison. Where labour is plentiful, wage rates are lower than in economies where it is scarce, so the cost the equipment has to beat is smaller. Where equipment is imported, it is paid for in a foreign currency, exposed to exchange-rate movement, and serviced from far away, so its true cost is above the list price and a breakdown costs more days than it would elsewhere. The volume at which capital becomes the cheaper route is therefore higher here than it would be in a country making its own machinery.

The strongest argument against staying is that labour cost per unit does not fall with volume, so if the firm wins a large standing order for one garment it will be undercut by a mechanised competitor on that line, and wage rates rise over time while equipment cost per unit falls with use. The judgement therefore changes if a single high-volume standard line emerges, or if wage rates rise sharply. The practical course is a mixed operation - mechanise the cutting room, where volume is shared across all lines, and keep assembly on labour - which is how most of the industry actually runs.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a recommendation is required, with the condition under which it changes.
Context: the answer must use both facts given - plentiful labour and imported equipment - and show why each shifts the comparison.
Criterion: the decisive factor is volume and variety, not the wage rate alone.
Counterargument: the failure of labour cost per unit to fall with volume must be addressed.
Condition: the answer must name what would change the judgement.

items.prompt: A Windhoek bakery makes 600 brown loaves, cleans its equipment, then makes 400 white loaves. A Namibian water bottler fills the same bottle on one line all week. Explain the difference between batch and flow production, using these two operations.

The bakery is batching: each run of loaves stops for a clean-down, which lets it offer several breads with modest equipment, at the price of time lost at each change. The bottler is using flow: its line does not stop for changeovers, giving a very low cost per bottle at high volume, but it needed a large outlay and allows almost no variety.

items.prompt: Explain the disadvantages of flow production.
items.canonical_answer: The commitment comes first and is large: a flow line requires heavy capital outlay before anything is produced, and the cost then has to be covered from whatever volume appears. The work is also repetitive, so motivation and quality of working life need active management if turnover and carelessness are not to rise.

items.prompt: A Namibian dairy currently bottles 200 crates a month of each of four flavoured milks, using one filling machine cleaned between products. A supermarket chain now offers a standing order for 15 000 crates a month of plain milk alone. Explain which production method suits each part of the business.

The four flavoured milks stay on batch production. Each is a small volume of a distinct specification, the machine is shared, and the cleaning between products is exactly the set-up that batching exists to spread; at 200 crates a flavour, no dedicated line could be justified, and job production would be absurd for identical crates.

The plain milk order suits flow production. 15 000 crates a month of one unchanging specification is high volume with no variety, which is the condition under which a continuous line is cheapest per unit and the large outlay can be spread thinly enough to be worth making. The two coexist: the dairy would run a dedicated line for the supermarket order and keep the shared batch machine for the flavours. What would make this the wrong answer is the security of the standing order - a line justified on 15 000 crates a month and fed 4 000 is a worse position than the batch machine the dairy already owns.

items.prompt: Analyse why cost per unit is higher under job production than under batch production.
items.canonical_answer: Start from the condition that both methods incur the same kind of preparation - setting up equipment, obtaining materials, briefing the worker - but recover it over different quantities. Under job production that preparation happens for a single item, because the next item is made to a different specification, so the whole of it is carried by one unit. Under batch production the same preparation serves a whole group, so each unit carries a fraction of it. The mechanism compounds through labour: job production uses skilled employees on a whole task, and skilled time is dearer per hour than the narrower work batching allows, while the learning gained on the first item is partly wasted when the next is different. The measurable consequence is a cost per unit that can be several times the batch figure, which reaches the price the business has to quote and therefore the market it can compete in. It also reaches the type of customer it serves: the job producer is pushed towards buyers who value the specification enough to pay for it, since it cannot win a customer choosing on price alone.

Mechanism: preparation and skilled time spread over one unit against many, with the learning effect.

items.prompt: A furniture manufacturer selling one standard kitchen unit is considering offering buyers a choice of eight door finishes through mass customisation. Evaluate whether it should.
items.canonical_answer:
It should offer the choice if the eight finishes can be applied at the last stage of the line and its order system can track which unit belongs to which customer - and it should not if either condition fails. The decisive criterion is where in the process the variation happens, because that is what determines whether mass customisation costs like flow production or like job production.

The case in favour is commercial. Mass customisation offers buyers a choice of specification without the unit cost of job production, so the manufacturer can reach customers who currently buy elsewhere because the standard unit does not suit their kitchen, while holding most of the cost advantage of its line. Applying the finish as the last operation means the first stages continue to run one identical product at full speed.

The case against is complexity. The product has to be designed as modules, and the system has to track which variant belongs to which order; the number of variants offered is limited by what that system can handle, and a tracking error produces a finished unit nobody ordered, which is scrapped or discounted. Eight finishes is eight times the component lines to hold and eight ways of getting it wrong.

On balance, with the variation at the end of the line and a system that can carry the order through, the move is worth making. The judgement reverses if the finish has to be applied before assembly, because the line then runs eight different products and the cost advantage that justified it disappears.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a plain recommendation with its condition.
Context: the answer must be argued for eight door finishes on one standard unit, not for choice in general.
Criterion: the decisive factor is where in the process the variation is introduced.
Counterargument: the tracking and complexity risk must be addressed with its consequence.
Condition: the answer must state what would reverse the judgement.

items.prompt: Explain why a change of production method usually costs a business output as well as money.

items.prompt: Explain the workforce problems a business faces when it moves from batch to flow production.
items.canonical_answer:
The skills the operation needs change, so staff have to be retrained, which costs money and takes people off production while it happens. More seriously, a move towards flow narrows many jobs to one repeated task: a batch operator who set up the machine, ran it and checked the output may end up doing a single operation on a moving line. Some employees experience that as a loss of skill and interest, and the consequence shows up as higher labour turnover and weaker motivation, which raises recruitment costs and lowers quality just when the new line needs care.

The change also usually alters the number of people required, so the business may face redundancy payments, statutory consultation with employees or their representatives, and a spell of poor industrial relations while the change is negotiated. Exact legal requirements for notice, consultation and compensation depend on the jurisdiction, so the cost of that part cannot be assumed from another country's rules.
marking_guidance: The limitation must be developed through the mechanism from narrowed jobs to turnover and quality.
The answer must reach the redundancy and consultation consequences, and must treat the legal requirements as jurisdiction-dependent rather than universal.

items.prompt: Analyse why the first months after a change of production method are the most expensive.

The measurable consequence is a squeeze on cash in the months after the change, which reaches the business's ability to meet its repayments and may force it to seek further finance at the moment its figures look worst. The squeeze eases as output per employee rises towards the planned level, which is why the length of the learning period is worth forecasting rather than assuming.

items.prompt: A bottling firm filling 9 000 crates a month in batches with 18 employees is installing a flow line costing N$3 200 000 that will need 11 employees and fill 15 000 crates a month. Explain the two largest risks it takes, using its own figures.

But that N$4.40 assumes 15 000 crates are sold. At the current 9 000, labour is N$66 000 / 9 000 = N$7.33 a crate, still lower, while the N$3 200 000 is being carried by 9 000 crates a month instead of 15 000. The investment was justified on a volume the firm does not yet have.

The second risk is the changeover itself. The batch machine has to come out while the line is installed and tested, so output falls during the change and the firm must build stock in advance or lose orders. Both risks bite at once: it is spending N$3 200 000 and producing less than usual in the same quarter, which is when a firm most needs its cash.

items.prompt: A manufacturer with seasonal demand and borrowed finance has decided to move from batch to flow production. Evaluate whether it should convert the whole plant at once or one line at a time.
items.canonical_answer:
It should convert one line at a time. The decisive criterion is the security of the volume that justifies the change, and for a business with seasonal demand and borrowed finance that volume is exactly what is uncertain, so the value of finding out before committing the rest is high.

Phasing works because it separates the risks. One line converted and proved first shows what the new method actually yields, how long the learning period lasts and what the defect rate settles at, while the existing method keeps running and the order book is still served. Employees can be consulted and retrained in smaller groups, which lowers the turnover and industrial-relations cost, and the finance is drawn in stages rather than in one commitment.

The strongest argument for converting at once is that the saving arrives sooner and in full, and that running two methods side by side costs money: duplicate supervision, two sets of materials handling, and a plant laid out for neither. A competitor converting wholesale reaches the lower cost first and may take the volume this firm was counting on. That argument would carry the decision if demand were steady and the finance were long-term - which is the condition that is absent here.

So: phase it, treating the extra cost as an insurance premium against a volume forecast that seasonality makes unreliable. The judgement changes if the firm secures a long-term contract at a known volume, in which case the certainty that justifies the full conversion has been bought.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a plain recommendation, not a balanced list.
Context: the answer must rest on this firm's seasonal demand and borrowed finance.
Criterion: the decisive factor is the security of the volume the change is justified on.
Counterargument: the cost of running two methods and the first-mover argument must be addressed.
Condition: the answer must name what would change the judgement - a long-term contract at a known volume.

items.prompt: Namib Sands Brick Works digs clay under licence, employs fourteen people, and fires bricks in two kilns bought with borrowed money. It sells bricks at N$9 each; the sand, cement and fuel bought in for each brick cost N$3.50. Explain, using this business, what is meant by the factors of production, the transformational process and added value.
items.canonical_answer:
Factors of production. Land is the clay pit and the water the licence permits; labour is the fourteen employees, of whom the kiln operators are the trained ones; capital is the press, the two kilns, the loader and the buildings, together with the borrowed money committed to them; enterprise is the owner's decision to borrow for a second kiln and the risk carried if the housing market slows. The four have to be combined: the clay without the kiln, or the kiln without the operators, produces nothing.

Transformational process. The inputs listed above enter, the transformation digs, mixes, presses, dries and fires them, and the outputs are saleable bricks plus cracked bricks and kiln waste. The change is physical and irreversible, which is why the firm measures the proportion cracking and feeds that back into how long the clay is dried and how hot the kiln is run.

Added value. Added value per brick = N$9.00 - N$3.50 = N$5.50, the difference between the selling price and the bought-in materials. That N$5.50 is what the operation itself created, and it has to cover the fourteen wages, the power, the repayments on the kilns and every other cost before anything is profit.
marking_guidance: Each of the three concepts must be stated as a point and then applied, not defined in the abstract.
The reason each concept matters to this business must be given: why the factors must be combined, why feedback is used, what the added value has to cover.
Context: each of the three sections must use the brickworks' own facts and figures.

items.prompt: Oshakati Packers employs 25 staff who packed 33 750 cartons last month, on a wage bill of N$168 750 and total operating costs of N$337 500. Its target is 1 400 cartons per employee per month. A consultant proposes a conveyor costing N$900 000 that would let 20 staff pack 36 000 cartons a month on a wage bill of N$135 000, with maintenance adding N$9 000 a month to other costs. Calculate labour productivity, labour cost per carton and average cost per carton now and under the proposal, and evaluate whether Oshakati should install the conveyor.
items.canonical_answer:
Now. Labour productivity = 33 750 / 25 = 1 350 cartons per employee per month, against a target of 1 400, so the operation is 50 cartons per employee short of it. Labour cost per carton = N$168 750 / 33 750 = N$5.00. Average cost per carton = N$337 500 / 33 750 = N$10.00.

Under the proposal. Labour productivity = 36 000 / 20 = 1 800 cartons per employee per month, which is above the target. Labour cost per carton = N$135 000 / 36 000 = N$3.75. Other costs are currently N$337 500 - N$168 750 = N$168 750, and the maintenance adds N$9 000, giving N$177 750; total costs become N$135 000 + N$177 750 = N$312 750, so average cost per carton = N$312 750 / 36 000 = N$8.69.

Judgement: install the conveyor, provided the extra 2 250 cartons a month can be sold or the five posts can genuinely be released. The decisive criterion is that condition, not the productivity figure. A rise from 1 350 to 1 800 cartons per employee is a genuine improvement, and average cost falls by N$1.31 a carton, which on 36 000 cartons is worth N$1.31 x 36 000 = N$47 160 a month. On that saving the N$900 000 is recovered in N$900 000 / 47 160 = 19.1 months. But the whole saving assumes both the volume and the smaller headcount. If Oshakati can sell only 33 750 cartons, the conveyor still saves wages but spreads N$900 000 over the old volume, and if the five posts cannot be removed the labour saving does not arrive at all.

The strongest argument against is the workforce cost of releasing five people: redundancy payments, consultation, and the effect on the twenty who remain, whose jobs become narrower. The conveyor also concentrates risk - a breakdown now stops the whole packing operation rather than one bench. The judgement changes if demand is seasonal, if the finance is short-term, or if the five staff can be redeployed rather than released, which would remove the strongest objection while keeping most of the volume gain.
marking_guidance: All six figures must be calculated with working shown, and the other-costs figure derived rather than assumed.
Judgement: the answer must recommend, not set out both cases and stop.
Context: the recommendation must rest on Oshakati's own volumes, headcount and target.
Criterion: the decisive factor is whether the extra output can be sold or the posts genuinely released.
Counterargument: the redundancy and single-point-of-failure risks must be addressed.
Condition: the answer must name what would change the judgement.

items.prompt: Plan an answer to: "Evaluate whether a growing Namibian food processor should move from labour intensive batch production to capital intensive flow production."
items.canonical_answer:
Opening position: the move is right only where the volume that justifies it is secure, and for a growing processor that security is the thing to establish before the equipment is ordered.

Paragraph 1 - the case for. At high and steady volumes a capital intensive flow operation tends to have the lower cost per unit, because heavy equipment cost is spread over many units and little labour time is used on each; the output is also more uniform, which is what an institutional buyer to a fixed specification is paying for. Develop with the point that uniformity may be the entry condition for supermarket supply, not merely a cost advantage.

Paragraph 2 - the case against, on cost behaviour. Labour cost can be reduced when demand falls; the equipment cost cannot. A move to flow raises the share of total cost that is fixed, so the processor reaches a loss at a level of demand that would previously have been survivable. Develop with the arithmetic: the same capital carried by fewer units raises cost per unit sharply.

Paragraph 3 - the transition. The problems of changing method are separate from the merits of the destination: capital committed before anything is earned, output lost during installation, retraining, redundancy and consultation costs, and a learning period in which output per employee starts below its eventual level.

Paragraph 4 - context that changes the answer. Where labour is plentiful and equipment imported, the volume at which capital becomes cheaper is higher than it would be elsewhere. Seasonal demand weakens the case; a signed long-term contract strengthens it.

Conclusion: recommend a phased move, converting one line and proving it before committing the rest, with the decisive criterion stated as the security of the volume. Name the counterargument - that phasing costs money and a competitor moving wholesale reaches the lower cost first - and the condition that reverses the recommendation: a long-term order at a known volume, which buys the certainty the full move needs.
marking_guidance: The plan must set out a line of argument, not a list of headings.
Judgement: a position must be taken in the opening and carried to the conclusion.
Context: the plan must use the Namibian facts - plentiful labour, imported equipment - as argument, not decoration.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be named as the security of the volume.
Counterargument: the first-mover and cost-of-phasing arguments must appear.
Condition: the plan must state what would reverse the recommendation.

items.prompt: Erongo Tanning treats 3 000 hides a month. It sells each finished hide at N$320, of which N$130 is the bought-in hide and chemicals. Its effluent is trucked to a treatment site at N$72 000 a month, and the regional authority has signalled that the charge will rise. A closed-loop water and chemical recovery system would cost N$1 500 000, cut effluent trucking to N$18 000 a month, and reduce bought-in chemicals by N$14 a hide, but would take four months to install, during which output would fall by a third. Analyse the impact of the system on the business and evaluate whether Erongo should install it.
items.canonical_answer:
Present position. Added value per hide = N$320 - N$130 = N$190, so monthly added value = N$190 x 3 000 = N$570 000, out of which the N$72 000 effluent charge is met.

The system's effect once running. Effluent trucking falls by N$72 000 - N$18 000 = N$54 000 a month. Chemicals fall by N$14 x 3 000 = N$42 000 a month. Total monthly saving = N$54 000 + N$42 000 = N$96 000, and added value per hide rises to N$320 - N$116 = N$204. Payback on the saving alone = N$1 500 000 / 96 000 = 15.6 months.

The cost of getting there. Output falls by a third for four months, so the firm loses about 1 000 hides a month of added value for four months: N$190 x 1 000 = N$190 000 a month, or N$760 000 in all, on top of the N$1 500 000 outlay. Cash and profit worsen substantially before they improve, which is the shape every sustainability measure of this kind takes.

Analysis. The saving is durable rather than one-off: it removes a real quantity of purchased input each month and continues for as long as the plant runs, which is what makes a 15.6-month payback meaningful. It also reduces exposure to the signalled rise in the treatment charge, since a firm trucking N$18 000 of effluent is hurt far less by a percentage increase than one trucking N$72 000. Against that, the transition cost is large and falls in one block, and an operation that cannot fund it will not reach the saving at all.

Recommendation: install it, provided the four-month output loss can be financed and customers held. The decisive criterion is the combination of a durable saving with a real reduction in regulatory exposure - the payback would justify it even without the second, and the second makes waiting actively risky, since the charge is expected to rise. The strongest argument against is the transition: N$760 000 of lost added value plus N$1 500 000 of outlay is a demand on cash that a tannery of this size may not be able to meet, and customers served late for four months may not return. The recommendation therefore depends on two conditions: finance arranged over a term longer than the payback, and the installation phased or scheduled into the slowest season so that less output is lost. If neither can be arranged, the right course is to negotiate the treatment contract and install the water recovery part alone, which takes a smaller share of the saving for a much smaller interruption.
marking_guidance: Every figure must be calculated with working shown, including the transition cost.
Judgement: a recommendation is required, not an account of both sides.
Context: the analysis must rest on Erongo's own volumes, charges and the signalled rise.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be named and distinguished from the payback calculation alone.
Counterargument: the transition cost and the risk to customers must be addressed with figures.
Condition: the answer must name the conditions the recommendation depends on and the fallback if they fail.

items.prompt: A distribution company pays its depot managers a bonus based on the labour productivity of their depot, measured as parcels handled per employee per month. Evaluate whether that is a sound basis for the bonus.
items.canonical_answer:
It is a poor basis on its own and should be used only alongside a quality and a cost measure. The decisive criterion is whether the figure is under the manager's control and measures what the company actually wants, and on both counts parcels per employee falls short.

Labour productivity is raised by better equipment as readily as by better management. A depot given a new sorting conveyor will show a rise that the manager did not produce, and a depot whose conveyor is out of service will show a fall the manager could not prevent, so the bonus rewards capital allocation rather than performance. The measure also counts quantity and not quality: parcels misrouted, damaged or delivered late are still in the count, so the fastest route to the bonus is to handle parcels less carefully. And a headcount that treats part-time and seasonal staff as whole employees understates the labour used, so a depot that meets a peak with casual staff looks worse than one that meets it with overtime.

The argument in favour is real and should not be dismissed: the figure is objective, cheap to compute and comparable across depots, which is more than can be said for most management measures, and a manager who improves layout and scheduling genuinely moves it.

So the judgement is to keep the measure but not to pay on it alone: pay on parcels per labour hour rather than per employee, hold equipment constant when comparing depots or compare each depot with its own past, and attach a condition on damage and mis-delivery rates. Without those changes the scheme buys speed and pays for it in claims.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a plain recommendation, with what should replace or supplement the measure.
Context: the answer must be argued for depot managers measured on parcels per employee, not for bonuses in general.
Criterion: the decisive factor is controllability and whether the measure captures what is wanted.
Counterargument: the genuine merits of the measure - objective, cheap, comparable - must be acknowledged.
Condition: the answer must name what would make the scheme sound.

items.prompt: A manufacturer proposes to judge its operations department on productivity alone, on the grounds that the other measures are harder to quantify. Evaluate that proposal.
items.canonical_answer:
The proposal should be rejected, and the reason is not that productivity is a bad measure but that it is one of four and the others move independently of it. The decisive criterion is that a single measure can be improved by changes that worsen the operation as a whole, and nothing in the measure itself reveals that.

Productivity asks how much output each unit of input yields. Efficiency asks how little resource is used for the output produced, effectiveness whether the objectives set were achieved, and sustainability whether the operation can be carried on. Running a line faster raises output per employee while giving each unit less time in the process, so the reject rate rises and resources used per saleable unit rise with it: productivity improves and efficiency worsens in the same week. A department judged on the first has been given a reason to make that trade.

The argument for the proposal is that a measure nobody can compute is not a measure, and productivity has the advantage of being countable. That is fair, and it points to the answer: efficiency can be quantified as average cost per unit, and effectiveness as performance against the objectives actually set, so the claim that only productivity is measurable is weaker than it looks.

The recommendation is to judge on productivity together with average cost per saleable unit and performance against the department's own objectives, weighting them according to what the business is trying to do this year. The judgement would change if the department had no control over quality or specification, in which case a narrow measure of what it does control would be fairer.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a plain recommendation on the proposal itself.
Context: the answer must address this manufacturer's stated reason - that the others are hard to quantify.
Criterion: the decisive factor is that one measure can improve while the operation worsens.
Counterargument: the measurability argument must be answered, not ignored.
Condition: the answer must name what would change the judgement.

items.prompt: A poultry producer can install a biogas digester that converts its waste into power, saving N$11 000 a month on purchased electricity for an outlay of N$660 000. Its waste is currently removed by a contractor at no charge. Evaluate whether it should install the digester.
items.canonical_answer:
It should install it if it expects to be operating on the same site for well beyond the payback period and can fund the outlay without straining its working capital; otherwise it should not, and the size of the saving is not by itself the reason either way.

Payback = N$660 000 / 11 000 = 60 months, which is five years. The decisive criterion is the relationship between that five years and the life of the equipment and the producer's tenure on the site. A digester with a twenty-year life on land the business owns is a straightforward investment: fifteen years of saving follow the payback. The same five years on a lease with seven years to run is a much thinner proposition.

The case in favour beyond the money is that the saving repeats - power not bought is not paid for every month the digester runs - and that it removes dependence on a waste contractor whose terms are currently free but need not stay so, and on an electricity supply whose price the producer does not control.

The strongest argument against is the cash profile. N$660 000 leaves the business before any of it returns, and there is retraining and a period of disruption while the digester is commissioned, so profit and cash worsen before they improve. A five-year payback is long enough that a producer with tight cash should not fund it from working capital.

The judgement changes if the waste contractor begins to charge, which would add to the monthly saving and shorten the payback, or if the producer can secure finance over a term longer than five years, which would let the saving service the borrowing rather than the business funding it.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a plain recommendation with the condition that carries it.
Context: the answer must use the N$660 000 and N$11 000 figures and the fact that waste removal is currently free.
Criterion: the decisive factor is the payback period set against equipment life and tenure.
Counterargument: the cash profile before the saving arrives must be addressed.
Condition: the answer must name what would change the judgement.

items.prompt: Analyse the effect on a labour intensive workshop of a 10% rise in the minimum wage.
items.canonical_answer:
Start from the condition that labour costs form the larger share of this workshop's total cost, which is what makes it labour intensive. The mechanism is that a wage rise passes straight into cost per unit with nothing in the operation to absorb it: there is no large body of equipment cost that stays still while wages rise, so the rise is felt on almost the whole cost base rather than a part of it. A workshop with a wage bill of N$90 000 a month producing 1 500 units carries N$90 000 / 1 500 = N$60 of labour in each unit. After the rise the bill is N$90 000 x 1.1 = N$99 000, so each unit carries N$99 000 / 1 500 = N$66, a rise of N$6.

The measurable consequence is a margin narrowed by N$6 a unit at an unchanged selling price, and the workshop has three responses, each with its own cost: raise the price and risk volume, absorb it and accept the thinner margin, or substitute equipment for some of the labour, which requires capital it may not have and time it does not get. The effect therefore reaches the profit of the business immediately and its factor mix over a longer horizon, since a sustained rise in the price of labour is exactly what pushes an operation towards capital. Employees are the other stakeholder, and for them the same change raises pay while raising the chance that the substitution eventually happens.
marking_guidance: Condition: labour is the larger share of total cost, which is what transmits the rise.
Mechanism: little equipment cost stays fixed, so the rise falls on nearly the whole cost base.
Consequence: cost per unit rises by a calculated amount, narrowing the margin.
The chain must reach the profit of the business and should identify the effect on employees or on the longer-term factor mix.

items.prompt: Two courier depots report last month: Oshakati handled 12 600 parcels with 14 drivers, Rundu handled 15 400 with 22 drivers. Explain which is the more productive and what would have to be true for the comparison to be fair.
items.canonical_answer:
Labour productivity = total output / number of employees. Oshakati: 12 600 / 14 = 900 parcels per driver per month. Rundu: 15 400 / 22 = 700 parcels per driver per month. Oshakati is the more productive, by 200 parcels a driver, even though Rundu handled more parcels in total - which is the difference between production and productivity.

For the comparison to be fair the two depots would have to be producing comparable output by comparable methods. Three things would have to hold. The drivers would have to work similar hours, since a headcount treats a part-timer as a whole employee and output per labour hour would be the safer measure if they do not. The parcels would have to be similar, because a depot delivering dense urban drops covers more in a day than one covering scattered rural addresses whatever the driver does. And the equipment would have to be comparable, since a depot with a sorting conveyor will show higher output per driver without its drivers working differently at all.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must compute and compare both depots' own figures.
Reasoning: the mechanism must explain why the totals mislead and what makes a comparison valid.
Conclusion: the answer must reach a named depot and state the conditions the comparison rests on.

items.prompt: A bakery changes over between products once per batch. A changeover occupies the oven for an hour, and oven time is costed at N$450 an hour. Calculate the set-up cost carried by each loaf in a batch of 600 and in a batch of 150, and explain what the difference shows about batch production.
items.canonical_answer:
Set-up cost per unit = cost of the set-up / number of units in the batch. Batch of 600: N$450 / 600 = N$0.75 a loaf. Batch of 150: N$450 / 150 = N$3.00 a loaf. The difference is N$2.25 a loaf on exactly the same changeover.

What it shows is where batch production's cost advantage comes from and where it stops. The set-up is a fixed amount spread across whatever the batch contains, so a large group carries it thinly and a small one barely spreads it at all. Batch production is cheaper per unit than job production for that reason, and it becomes less so as batches shrink towards single items.
marking_guidance: Formula: set-up cost per unit = cost of the set-up / units in the batch.
Substitution must be shown for both batch sizes.
Units: currency per loaf on every figure.
Interpretation: the answer must say what the difference means for batch production, not merely state it.
